transcript.content: Hello, I'm Dr. Smith. It's nice to meet you; could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. Smith, it's nice to meet you too, though to be perfectly honest, I'm not entirely sure I need to be here, but my supervisor insisted. See, I work as a personal care aide, taking care of elderly folks mostly, which is a really big responsibility, you know? You really have to be on your toes because they can slip and fall, and if they fall, it's a whole disaster—hip fractures, hospital visits, paperwork, the works. 

So anyway, we were having this staff meeting last Tuesday, or maybe it was Wednesday... no, Tuesday, because it was right after the lunch shift. We were sitting around talking about safety protocols, and I guess... I guess what brings me in is I just got really, really worked up about it. I mean, it's life or death for some of these clients! So I stood up, and I started acting out this whole fall-prevention drill right there in the middle of the room. I grabbed a couple of the folding chairs to show how to block a sliding fall, and I was waving my arms around to demonstrate how you have to shift your center of gravity, just really getting into the mechanics of it all to make sure everyone understood. 

And the thing is, I just kept going. People were looking at me kind of funny, and my manager told me to sit down, like, three or four times, but I couldn't seem to stop. I just had to finish showing them exactly how it needed to be done, even with folks telling me to sit down and lower my voice. I was just in the zone with it, but they thought it was too much, so... now here I am.
Outside of that meeting, have you felt like you've been in an unusually good mood or had much more energy than usual for several days in a row lately?

Well, yeah, I guess you could say that. It’s not just the meeting, honestly. There are these stretches, you know? Like, days at a time where I just wake up and I feel... I don't know, just really bright. Just completely fired up and ready to take on the whole world. It’s like everything is finally lining up perfectly, like all the gears in my head are finally catching and turning exactly how they're supposed to, and I don't even need my coffee to get going. I'll get so much done, whether it's at my apartment or at work. I'll be doing extra rounds, checking on Mrs. Higgins, making sure Mr. Abernathy has his water pitcher filled to the exact brim because hydration is absolutely key for the elderly, right? I just have all this fuel in the tank, and it feels amazing to just go, go, go.

But the thing is... and this is where it gets a little tricky, I guess, and maybe why my supervisor got so on my case. Because I'm moving so fast and feeling so on top of things, if someone tries to slow me down, or if they start questioning what I'm doing—like asking why I'm reorganizing the supply closet or why I'm explaining the fall protocols so passionately—I just... I snap. I snap way harder than I mean to. It’s like they’re throwing a wrench right into those gears I was talking about. I really don't mean to get nasty with anybody, but when you see everything so clearly and someone else is just dragging their feet or telling you to sit down and be quiet, it just completely sets me off. So yeah, I feel fantastic, like a million bucks, right up until someone gets in my way or doubts me, and then it's just... I just lose my temper with them.

During these periods where you feel like you have all this extra energy, have you ever felt like you were receiving special messages, or seen or heard things that other people around you didn't seem to notice?

Well, yes, actually, and it's funny you bring that up because it's... it's a lot to process, to be honest. See, when I get into those stretches—those really fired-up days where I'm just buzzing, you know? Where I'm only sleeping maybe two, three hours a night because who needs sleep when you have so much to accomplish, right? I'll be up making these massive, detailed plans for how to completely overhaul the facility's safety protocols, drafting these ten-page memos in my head. 

But during those exact same times, when I'm just running on all cylinders... I start hearing things. Not like, just a random noise, but actual calls. Like someone calling out my name or giving me instructions, clear as a bell, but there's nobody in the hallway. I'll be doing my rounds at 2 AM, and I'll hear this voice, and I'll turn around, and the corridor is completely empty. Just the hum of the fluorescent lights. And the other staff, they never hear it. I've asked them, "Did you hear someone calling for assistance in room 4B?" and they just look at me like I'm crazy. 

And on top of that, it's not just the voices. I start getting this overwhelming feeling... this absolute certainty that my supervisor—the one who made me come here—is actually setting traps for me. Like, literal traps to get me fired or worse. I'll notice how she leaves a mop bucket slightly out of place near the nurses' station, or how she schedules me for back-to-back shifts with the most difficult clients, and I just know, I *know* in my gut, that it's a coordinated effort to trip me up. It all feels so connected when I'm in that state, the voices and the traps, like it's all part of this big test that I have to navigate while I'm trying to implement all my new plans. It's just... it's exhausting, honestly, having to be so vigilant while I'm also trying to do so much good.
Outside of these high-energy periods you've described, have you ever experienced significant stretches of time where you felt deeply down, hopeless, or lost interest in the things you usually enjoy?

Well, no, not really. I mean, I don't get those deep, dark slumps you hear people talk about on those daytime talk shows, you know? Where they just pull the covers up over their heads and can't even drag themselves to the kitchen to make a piece of toast. I don't have those stretches where everything just feels gray and heavy and useless. 

I mean, sure, sometimes I might feel a little tired after one of those really intense, high-energy runs where I've been working double shifts and reorganizing the entire supply closet and writing those memos in my head all night. Naturally, your body has to catch up eventually, right? You can't run an engine at a hundred miles an hour forever without it needing a little cool-down period. So maybe I'll have a day where I just want to sit on the couch and watch some TV and not talk to anybody, just kind of recharge the batteries, so to speak. 

But it's never that deep, hopeless feeling you're asking about. I never lose interest in my work or my clients. Even when I'm just having a regular, middle-of-the-road day, I still care about Mrs. Higgins and Mr. Abernathy. I still want to make sure they're safe and taken care of. I don't get that whole 'what's the point of it all' mindset. I always know what the point is. It's just that sometimes I'm tackling the point with a million volts of electricity, and other times I'm just doing it at a normal, steady pace. But yeah, no big, long stretches of feeling completely down in the dumps or hopeless. That's just not really my thing.

When you are in those 'middle-of-the-road' periods where you aren't feeling that intense energy or staying up all night, do those voices you hear or those feelings that your supervisor is setting traps for you still happen?

Well, yeah... it’s funny you ask that, because, actually, yes. There was this one stretch not too long ago where things had really leveled out for me. I was having a really calm period, you know? I was actually sleeping normally for once—getting a solid seven or eight hours, going to bed at a decent time instead of being up till dawn. And I wasn't rushing around with all those massive projects either, no overhauling the safety protocols or reorganizing the closets or anything like that. Just going in, doing my job, and coming home. 

But the thing is... for several weeks during that totally normal, calm stretch, that other stuff was still happening. I'd be walking down the hall, totally rested, no racing thoughts at all, and I'd still hear my name being called out. Just out of nowhere, clear as day, when nobody was around. 

And the stuff with my supervisor... it actually felt like it kind of spread out, because I stayed absolutely convinced that people at work were keeping notes on me. I’d see one of the other aides jotting something down on a clipboard near the nurses' station, and even though my brain wasn't buzzing with all that extra energy, I just knew in my gut they were documenting my every move, writing down what time I took my break or how long I spent in a room, building some kind of file on me. 

It’s strange, right? Because you’d think if the engine cools down, all the extra noise would stop with it. But no, for weeks I was sleeping fine and taking it easy, but I was still hearing my name echoing in the halls and constantly looking over my shoulder, worrying about these secret notes everyone was keeping on me. It really makes you wonder how it all connects, because I was feeling completely even-keeled otherwise, but I still couldn't shake that feeling of being watched and documented.
